questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Display the list itself, in the form [8, 3, 5, 1, 9].

teach.say: A list holds many values in one variable. Start with an empty list and .append() each value onto the end of it.

brief: Store them as whole numbers.
Keep them in the order they were typed.
Print the list itself, square brackets and commas and all.
questions.starter: # Read five numbers into a list, then print the list

tests.why: The list keeps the order the numbers were typed in.
A list keeps every item, even when two of them are the same.
Quote marks round the values mean the text from input() was stored instead of being cast with int().

questions.fb: Start with an empty list and .append() each value as you read it - printing the list shows the brackets and the commas for you.

questions.q: Ask the user for five words, one on each line. Store them in a list. Display the list itself, in the form ['red', 'blue', 'green', 'teal', 'grey'].
brief: Keep them in the order they were typed.
Print the list itself, brackets and quote marks and all.
questions.starter: # Read five words into a list, then print the list

tests.why: The quote marks appear because the items are strings, and printing the list puts them there for you.
Repeats are kept: a list holds every item, even when they are all the same.
A line with no brackets means the words were joined together instead of being kept in a list.

questions.fb: A list of words prints with quote marks round each item, because each one is a string.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many whole numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Display the list itself, in the form [8, 3, 5].
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow, which is never less than 1.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
The first number read is not one of them.
questions.starter: # Read as many numbers as the first line says

tests.why: Three numbers follow the count, so the list holds three items.
A list of one item still prints its brackets. A list of two means the count was appended as well.
A 0 is an item like any other, and the loop runs as many times as the first line says.
Negative numbers are stored the same way. A crash here means the loop read more lines than were typed.

questions.fb: range() can count up to a number read from the user, so the length of the list is decided while the program runs.

questions.q: Ask the user for four words, one on each line. Then ask for a position counting from 0. Store the words in a list. Display [the word at that position] and nothing else.

teach.say: A list is indexed like a string: box[0] is the first item and box[1] the second.

brief: The user types in five lines: four words, then a position counting from 0.
The position is always one the list has.
questions.starter: # Read four words, then print the one at that position

tests.why: Position 2 is the third item, because the counting starts at 0.
Position 0 is the first item. Printing hammer means position 1 was treated as the first item.
Four items means 3 is the last position, and adding 1 would run off the end of the list.
Different words, so a word typed in by hand fails here.

questions.fb: A list of four items has positions 0 to 3, so the last position is always one less than the length.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Display [the first one]. Then display [the last one] on the next line.

teach.say: len() counts the items in a list, the same way it counts the characters in a string, so the last position is len() - 1.

brief: Take the last one from the list using its length, not by typing the position in yourself.
Two lines of output.
questions.starter: # The first item, then the last one

tests.why: The first item is at position 0 and the last at len() - 1.
The last item is the one at len() - 1. Using len() itself goes one past the end and crashes.
The first and the last, not the first two: a second line of 5 means position 1 was printed.

questions.fb: The first item is at position 0 and the last at len() - 1, so the length is what finds the end of any list.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Then ask for a position counting from 0. Store the numbers in a list. Display [the number at that position]. Display no such position instead when the list has no item there.
brief: The user types in six lines: five whole numbers, then a position.
Positions count from 0, and are never below 0.
Print exactly: no such position
questions.starter: # Print the item at that position, if there is one

tests.why: Position 2 is the third item, and it is a position the list has, so the number is printed.
Five items means 4 is the highest position. Refusing it means the test was p < len(nums) - 1 instead of p < len(nums).
Position 5 is one past the end: there are five items but the last position is 4.
Position 0 is the first item. Printing 9 means the positions were counted from 1.

questions.fb: A list of n items has positions 0 to n - 1, so test the position against len() before you use it.

questions.q: Ask the user for four words, one on each line. Store them in a list. Display a line for each word, in the form [word] [how many letters it has].

teach.say: A for loop over a list hands you each item in turn, so you never need a position number for this job.

brief: One line per word, in the order they were typed.
One space between the word and the number.
questions.starter: # Print each word with its length

tests.why: One line per item, the word first and the length second, in the typed order.
Four lines even when every length is the same, because the loop runs once for every item.
One line only means the print came after the loop instead of inside it - check the indentation.

questions.fb: A for loop over a list hands you the items one at a time, so no position number is needed for this job.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Display a line for each number, in the form [position] [number], with the positions counting from 0.

teach.say: range(len(box)) counts the positions of a list, so box[i] is the item the loop is on.

brief: One line per number, in the order they were typed.
One space between the position and the number.
questions.starter: # Loop over the positions, not the items

tests.why: The first line must be 0 7. If it says 1 7 the positions were counted from 1.
With every number the same only the positions change, which shows plainly that they run 0 to 4.
range(len(nums)) gives 0 up to 4 for five items, while range(1, len(nums)) would miss the first one.

questions.fb: range(len(nums)) counts the positions, so nums[i] is the item at the position the loop is on.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Count how many of them are 10 or more. Display [the count] and nothing else.
brief: Exactly 10 counts as 10 or more.
One line of output.

tests.why: Three of the five reach 10, and only the count is printed.
None of them reaches 10, so the counter stays at 0 and that 0 still has to be printed.
Exactly 10 counts, so four of them do. A 1 here means > 10 was used instead of >= 10.
All five count. A 1 means the counter was set back to 0 inside the loop instead of before it.

questions.fb: A counter with an if inside the loop counts only the items that pass the test.

questions.q: Ask the user for four words, one on each line. Store them in a list. Then ask for one more word. Append that word onto the same list. Display every item, one on each line.
brief: Append onto that same list - do not build a second one.
One line per item, in the order they are in the list.
questions.starter: # Four words, then one more on the end

tests.why: .append() puts an item on the end, so the fifth word comes after the four already there.
If an item is missing, the list was replaced with the new value instead of being appended to.
A repeated word is appended like any other, because .append() never checks whether the item is there already.

questions.fb: words.append(x) changes the list you already have, so there is nothing to assign it back to.

questions.q: Ask the user for five words, one on each line. Store them in a list. Then ask for a word to remove. Take that word out of the list. Display every remaining word, one on each line.

teach.say: box.remove(v) takes the value v out of the list and makes the list shorter straight away.

brief: The word to remove is always one the list holds.
One line per remaining word, in the order they are in the list.
questions.starter: # Take one word out of the list by its value

tests.why: Four words are left and they keep their order, with the gap closed up where rose was.
Removing the first item leaves four, and everything after it moves up one place.
Removing the last item leaves four. Five lines means the list was printed before the removal.
.remove() takes out the first match only, so one oak is still there.

questions.fb: .remove() is given the value to take out, and the list is shorter from that moment on.

questions.q: Ask the user for five words, one on each line. Store them in a list. Then ask for a position counting from 0. Delete the item at that position. Display every remaining word, one on each line.

teach.say: del box[i] takes out the item at position i, so everything after it moves up one place.

brief: The position is always one the list has.
One line per remaining word, in the order they are in the list.
questions.starter: # Take one word out of the list by its position

tests.why: Position 2 is the third item, because the counting starts at 0.
Position 0 is the first item. Losing ivy instead means the positions were counted from 1.
Five items means 4 is the last position, and this is where going one too far crashes.
del is given a position and not a value, so it takes the second oak because that is what sits at position 2.

questions.fb: del is given the position to take out while .remove() is given the value, and mixing the two up is the usual slip here.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Add them up. Display [the total] and nothing else.
brief: The numbers may be negative.
One line of output.

tests.why: All five are added, so the total grows on every turn of the loop.
All zeros still total 0, and that 0 has to be printed. A running total that starts at 1 gets this wrong.
A negative number lowers the total, so write total = total + n rather than adding only the large ones.
A 100 here means only the first item was added, or the total was printed inside the loop.

questions.fb: Set the total to 0 before the loop, add each item inside the loop, and print it once the loop has finished.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Work out their average. Round it to 1 decimal place. Display [the average] and nothing else, so 5 shows as 5.0.

teach.say: len(nums) is how many items a list holds, so dividing the total by it gives an average that works for any list. / always gives a real number.

brief: Divide the total by how many items the list holds, not by a number of your own.
Round the average to 1 decimal place.
questions.starter: # Total the list, then work out the average

tests.why: The total is 25 and there are five items, and / always gives a real number, so 5.0 and not 5.
Round to one decimal place with round(total / len(nums), 1), because the raw division gives a long run of digits for other data.
If the answer is out, check the division used the length of the list and not a number typed in by hand.
All zeros average 0.0, and a plain 0 does not match, because division always gives a real number.

questions.fb: The average is the finished total divided by len(list), worked out once the loop has ended.

questions.q: Ask the user for seven whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Find the largest with a loop of your own, not with max(). Display [the largest] and nothing else.
brief: The numbers may be negative.
They may all be the same.
Find the largest yourself rather than using max().

tests.why: The largest is in the middle of the list, so it has to be remembered as the loop goes rather than taken from either end.
When every number is the same it is already the largest, and nothing ever replaces it.
All seven are negative, so a largest that started at 0 would wrongly report 0. Start it at the first item instead.
The largest is the very first item, so a loop that skipped the first item would miss it.

questions.fb: Start the answer at the first item, then compare every item against it in turn - the first item is the only safe starting guess.
forbid: The point of this question is the loop - find the largest yourself rather than using max().

questions.q: Ask the user for eight whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Add them up. Work out their average. Round the average to 1 decimal place. Display [the total]. Then display [the average] on the next line.
brief: Divide the total by how many items the list holds.
Round the average to 1 decimal place, so 5 shows as 5.0.

tests.why: The total is printed as a whole number and the average rounded to one decimal place.
Every item the same still needs both lines, and / gives a real number, so 11.0 and not 11.
A long run of decimals on the second line means the round() is missing.
All zeros give a total of 0 and an average of 0.0, and both lines still have to print.

questions.fb: The total grows inside the loop and the average is worked out after it, from the finished total and the length of the list.

questions.q: Ask the user for seven whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Find the largest with a loop of your own, not with max(). Find the smallest with a loop of your own, not with min(). Display [the largest]. Then display [the smallest] on the next line.
brief: The numbers may be negative.
They may all be the same.
Largest first, smallest second.
Find them yourself rather than using max() or min().
questions.starter: # Find the largest and the smallest yourself

tests.why: Largest first, smallest second, and printing them the other way round is the easiest mark to lose here.
When every number is the same it is both the largest and the smallest.
All seven are negative, so starting the largest at 0 would wrongly report 0. Start both answers at the first item.
The largest and the smallest are both near the start, so a loop that began part way along would miss them both.

questions.fb: Start both answers at the first item and compare every item against both of them in turn.
forbid: The point of this question is the loop - find the largest yourself rather than using max().
The point of this question is the loop - find the smallest yourself rather than using min().

questions.q: Ask the user for eight whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list. Count how many of them are 12 or more. Find the position of the largest, counting from 0. Display [the count]. Then display [the position of the largest] on the next line.
brief: Exactly 12 counts as 12 or more.
When two items are equally large, the earlier position wins.
Find the position yourself rather than using max() or .index().
questions.starter: # How many reach 12, and where the largest one sits

tests.why: Five items reach 12, and the largest is the third one, which is position 2 - position 3 means the counting started at 1.
Nothing reaches 12, so the count is 0, and with every item equal the first one is the largest, which is position 0.
Two items are 20 and the earlier one wins, so compare with > and not >= when you replace the best position.
Exactly 12 counts, so the count is 4, and a 0 there means > 12 was used instead of >= 12.
The largest is the very last item, position 7, so a loop that stops one short of the end never sees it.

questions.fb: Two jobs over the same list: a counter with a condition, and a remembered position that is replaced only by a strictly larger item.
forbid: Find the largest with a loop of your own rather than using max().
Find the position of the largest as you go rather than looking it up with .index().
